chapterTitle: Project Panama: Foreign Function & Memory API

beats.headline: Why is JNI finally dying?
beats.subline: Native interop used to be a nightmare of C stubs and memory leaks. Project Panama changes the game.
beats.narration: For years, Java native interop meant brittle JNI glue or the dangerous sun dot misc Unsafe. Both are legacy tech. Project Panama’s FFM API is the modern, safe, and performant replacement.

beats.title: FFM API Architecture
beats.subtitle: Bridging Java to Native Memory
beats.narration: The FFM API gives us three pillars. Arenas manage memory lifecycles deterministically. MemorySegments provide bounds-checked access to off-heap memory. And the Linker binds C functions directly to Java code.

beats.title: The Native Access Flag
beats.caption: Security for native calls
beats.narration: Because native calls bypass Java safety, you must opt-in using the enable-native-access flag. In production, replace ALL-UNNAMED with your specific module name to keep your dependencies sandboxed.

beats.title: Deterministic Allocation

steps.explanation: Fastest option: single-thread access, zero sync overhead.
No more waiting for GC to free native memory.

beats.narration: Arenas solve the non-deterministic cleanup of old direct buffers. Using try-with-resources, memory is freed the moment the block exits. No GC pressure, no memory leaks.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 2): Spatial and Temporal Safety →
beats.narration: That's the foundation. In Part 2, we look at how MemorySegments prevent the crashes that plagued Unsafe for decades.

beats.headline: Can you crash the JVM with FFM?
beats.subline: Unsafe allowed arbitrary memory access. FFM forces safety without sacrificing raw performance.
beats.narration: Unsafe was a loaded gun. FFM is a professional tool. It enforces spatial and temporal safety so you can't read garbage or corrupt memory, even when working off-heap.

beats.title: Unsafe vs. MemorySegment
beats.narration: Unsafe just writes to an address. If you're wrong, the JVM crashes. MemorySegment tracks bounds. If you step outside, it throws a controlled exception instead of taking down the whole process.

beats.title: Temporal Safety

steps.explanation: Invalidates all segments associated with this scope.
Prevents use-after-free bugs common in native code.

beats.narration: Temporal safety is just as critical. Once an arena closes, all associated segments are invalidated. Any attempt to access them throws an exception, stopping use-after-free bugs in their tracks.

beats.title: Thread Confinement
beats.subtitle: Performance through isolation
beats.narration: Confined arenas are the fastest because they forbid cross-thread access, removing synchronization overhead. Shared arenas allow multi-threaded work, using lightweight handshakes to ensure safety during closure.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
beats.narration: Safety is handled. In Part 3, we see how to map complex C structs into Java using MemoryLayouts and VarHandles.

beats.headline: Stop calculating byte offsets manually.
beats.subline: C structs have padding and alignment rules. Java can now handle them declaratively.
beats.narration: Manually calculating byte offsets for C structs is a recipe for disaster. FFM uses MemoryLayouts to define the structure, and VarHandles to access the data safely.

beats.title: Defining a Struct

steps.explanation: Declarative definition of the C memory map.

beats.narration: Define your layout once. You can mix primitives and add padding to match C alignment rules exactly. This keeps your Java code clean and prevents alignment bugs.

beats.title: Accessing with VarHandle

steps.explanation: Compiled into efficient machine code by C2.
Supports indexing into arrays of structs.

beats.narration: VarHandles are the glue. They turn field names into efficient load and store instructions. C2 optimizes these so well they're nearly as fast as native field access.

beats.title: The jextract Tool
beats.caption: Auto-generate bindings
beats.narration: Don't write layouts by hand for large libraries. The jextract tool parses your C header files and generates all the Java bindings for you. It's the standard way to bridge big APIs.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
beats.narration: Layouts are solid. In Part 4, we finish by calling native C functions and passing Java callbacks back to C.

beats.headline: Call C functions without writing C.
beats.subline: The Linker bridge connects Java directly to the C ABI. No more JNI overhead.
beats.narration: The final piece is the Linker. It lets you call C functions and pass Java methods as callbacks. It’s all pure Java, with zero native build pipelines required.

beats.title: Downcall: Java to C

steps.explanation: Knows the host platform's C ABI.
Maps Java types to C types.

beats.narration: To call a C function, look up the symbol, define the signature with a descriptor, and get a MethodHandle. It’s type-safe and incredibly fast.

beats.title: Upcall: C to Java

steps.explanation: Stub lifetime is tied to the arena.

beats.narration: Upcalls are just as easy. Wrap a Java MethodHandle in an upcallStub, and you get a native function pointer you can pass to any C library. It’s perfect for custom comparators.

beats.title: Mapped Memory Upgrades
beats.narration: Finally, FFM fixes file I/O. MappedSegments break the 2GB limit and provide deterministic unmapping. It's the ultimate tool for high-performance databases and journals.

beats.title: Chapter Complete
beats.narration: You've mastered Project Panama. Check the branch below to run the native interop labs yourself. See you in the next level.
